items.prompt: What does Big O notation describe about an algorithm?

options.label: How its running time or memory grows as input size grows
The number of lines of source code needed to implement it
The fastest possible time it could take on its best input
The exact number of seconds it takes on one computer

rubric: Big O describes growth rate with input size.
Distractors confuse it with wall-clock time or code size.

items.prompt: Which precondition must hold for binary search to work on an array?

options.label: The array must be sorted
The array must be even
The array must have no repeats
The array must hold only integers

rubric: Binary search relies on sorted order to discard half.
Distractors add unrelated requirements.

items.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search on n items?

options.label: O(n)
O(log n)

rubric: Linear search may check every item.
O(log n) belongs to binary search.

items.prompt: In recursion, what is the base case?

options.label: The condition where the function stops calling itself
The first call made to the function from outside code
The step where the function splits the problem smaller
The case that calls itself the most times in a run

rubric: Base case ends recursion without a further call.
Distractors confuse it with the initial call.

items.prompt: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly swaps adjacent items that are out of order?

options.label: Bubble sort
Binary search
Merge sort
Quick select

rubric: Bubble sort swaps adjacent pairs.
Merge sort merges sorted halves; binary search is not a sort.

items.prompt: Which of these are standard sorting algorithms? Select all that apply.

options.label: Binary search
Merge sort
Selection sort
Insertion sort

rubric: Merge, insertion and selection sorts order data.
Binary search finds items; it does not sort.

items.prompt: A student is told that an algorithm solves a problem by breaking it into smaller copies of the same problem and combining results. The student must name the technique. Which term fits?

options.label: Divide and conquer
Random sampling
Exhaustive search
Sequential scanning

rubric: Splitting into subproblems and combining is divide and conquer.
Brute force tries all possibilities without splitting.

items.prompt: Why is O(log n) search on a sorted array faster than O(n) for large n?

options.label: It skips the first half of the array every time
Each step checks two items at once
Each step discards half of the remaining items
It stores every item in a hash table first

rubric: Halving gives logarithmic steps.
Distractors misdescribe the process.

items.prompt: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

options.label: The compiler turns it into a loop automatically
It returns zero or null after the first call
It keeps calling itself until the stack overflows
It runs once and then stops when no work is found

rubric: Without a base case, calls pile up until overflow.
Distractors assume automatic stopping.

items.prompt: Which running time makes an algorithm slowest when n gets very large?

options.label: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)

rubric: Exponential growth outpaces the others.
Learners often think n log n is worse.

items.prompt: A loop runs through a list of n items once, doing a constant amount of work each time. What is its time complexity?

options.label: O(log n)
O(n)

rubric: One pass with constant work is linear.
O(1) ignores the loop.

items.prompt: Why does dynamic programming store results of subproblems?

options.label: To avoid recomputing the same subproblem
To sort the subproblems by size before solving them
To use less memory than plain recursion would need
To split the problem into independent halves

rubric: Storing results avoids repeated work.
It often uses more memory, not less.

items.prompt: Which statements about merge sort are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: It sorts in place using O(1) extra memory
Its time complexity is O(n^2) in every case
It splits the list into halves and merges sorted halves
Its time complexity is O(n log n)

rubric: Merge sort uses divide and merge with O(n log n) time.
It needs extra memory, and it is not quadratic.

items.prompt: A programmer writes a nested loop where both loops run n times, doing constant work in the inner body. A friend says the code takes about n times n steps. How should the complexity be described?

options.label: O(n^2), since the body runs n times per pass
O(2n), since the two loops run one after the other
O(log n), since each pass repeats the same step
O(n), since constant work per step is dropped

rubric: Nested loops multiply, giving n^2.
Distractors add the loops instead of multiplying.

items.prompt: Why does binary search require the input array to be sorted?

options.label: Comparing with the middle element lets it discard half the range, which is only valid if order is known
Sorting makes every element unique, so a comparison with the middle element gives a reliable result every time
It needs sorted data so that it can count the elements before it starts, and the count fixes the middle index
It copies the array into a balanced tree first, and building that tree only works when the input is sorted

rubric: Discarding half the range relies on ordering.
Distractors invent unrelated requirements such as uniqueness or tree building.

items.prompt: What does it mean to say an algorithm runs in O(n^2) time?

options.label: It always performs exactly n squared basic operations, no more and no fewer, on every input of size n
Its running time grows roughly in proportion to the square of the input size
It takes two seconds for every input of size n
Its running time roughly doubles each time the input size increases by one more item

rubric: Big O describes growth rate as input grows.
Distractors confuse it with exact counts, fixed time, or exponential growth.

items.prompt: A recursive function has no base case. What will most likely happen when it is called?

options.label: It switches to a loop once the recursion gets deep enough
It runs once and then stops because nothing tells it to continue
It keeps calling itself until the call stack overflows
It returns zero after the first call finishes, as a default value

rubric: Without a base case recursion never terminates and exhausts the stack.
Distractors assume implicit termination.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why merge sort is described as a divide-and-conquer algorithm?

options.label: It splits the list into halves, sorts each half, then merges the results
It picks a pivot and moves smaller items to its left in one pass
It inserts each item into its place in a growing sorted prefix
It repeatedly swaps neighbouring items until none are out of order

rubric: Merge sort splits, recurses, and merges.
Distractors describe quicksort, bubble sort and insertion sort.

items.prompt: How does dynamic programming speed up a recursive solution such as naive Fibonacci?

options.label: It splits the problem into independent halves that never repeat, so no work is shared
It guesses the answer and checks it against the recursive result
It replaces the recursion with a faster comparison sort of the inputs
It stores results of overlapping subproblems so each is computed once

rubric: DP reuses stored answers to overlapping subproblems.
Distractors confuse it with sorting or divide and conquer on independent parts.

items.prompt: Which of these are true of a stable sorting algorithm? Select all that apply.

options.label: It always runs in O(n) time
Sorting by surname after sorting by first name keeps first-name order among equal surnames
Equal elements keep their original relative order
It never uses extra memory

rubric: Stability preserves order of equal keys, enabling multi-key sorting.
Distractors conflate stability with speed or memory.

items.prompt: A teammate says their function that checks each item in a list against every other item to find duplicates is fine because it works on their 20-item test list. The production list will hold 100,000 items. Which concern best reflects complexity analysis?

options.label: Nothing changes, since correct code runs equally fast at any size
The O(n^2) comparisons will grow to billions, so small tests hide the slowdown
The function will return wrong answers because large lists contain more duplicates
The function will use less memory as the list grows, causing errors

rubric: Quadratic growth makes large inputs far slower.
Distractors ignore growth rate or invent correctness issues.

items.prompt: Binary search runs on the sorted array `[2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38]` looking for 23, with low=0, high=6 and mid=(low+high)//2. What is the next range after the first comparison?

options.label: low=4, high=6
low=3, high=6
low=0, high=2
low=4, high=5

rubric: mid=3 holds 12; 23>12 so low=mid+1=4.
Distractors keep the wrong half or fail to skip mid.

items.prompt: What does `f(4)` return? `def f(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else n * f(n-1)`
rubric: Distractors confuse with sum, square, or partial product.

items.prompt: What is the time complexity of this code? `for i in range(n): for j in range(n): count += 1`

options.label: O(2n)
O(log n)
O(n)

rubric: Nested loops each run n times, giving n*n.
Distractors add the loops or assume halving.

items.prompt: Using one pass of bubble sort (swapping adjacent out-of-order pairs left to right) on `[4, 2, 5, 1]`, what is the list afterwards?
rubric: Swap 4,2; keep 4,5; swap 5,1 gives [2,4,1,5].
Distractors skip the last swap or fully sort.

items.prompt: Using the bottom-up recurrence `ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)` with ways(1)=1 and ways(2)=2 for climbing stairs with 1 or 2 steps, what is ways(5)?
rubric: Distractors are off-by-one indexing or wrong sums.

items.prompt: You must find a name in an unsorted list of 1,000 names once. Which approaches would work correctly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Check only the middle element
Binary search directly on the unsorted list
Linear search through the list
Sort the list, then use binary search

rubric: Linear search and sort-then-search are both correct.
Binary search on unsorted data or checking one element can miss the name.

items.prompt: You need the minimum number of coins to make 6 using coin values 1, 3 and 4. A classmate uses the greedy rule of taking the largest coin that fits. Which result shows what the correct answer is and what greedy gives?

options.label: Best is 2 coins (4+1+1); greedy gives 3 coins (3+3)
Best is 3 coins (4+1+1); greedy gives 2 coins (3+3)
Best is 2 coins (3+3); greedy gives 3 coins (4+1+1)
Both give 2 coins (3+3)

rubric: Greedy takes 4 then 1+1; optimum is 3+3.
Distractors swap the results or miscount coins.

items.prompt: Binary search runs on `[2,5,8,12,16,23,38,56,72,91]` with `lo=0`, `hi=9`, `mid=(lo+hi)//2`, looking for 23. In which order are the indices examined as `mid`?
rubric: Mid 4 holds 16 (go right), mid 7 holds 56 (go left, hi=6), mid 5 holds 23.
Distractors come from wrong bound updates or wrong integer-division rounding.

items.prompt: A divide-and-conquer algorithm splits a problem of size n into 3 subproblems of size n/2 and does O(n) extra work to combine them. What is its running time?

options.label: O(n log n)
O(n^(log2 3)), about O(n^1.58)

rubric: a=3, b=2, f(n)=n, so the leaves dominate and T(n)=O(n^(log_2 3)).
O(n log n) comes from assuming every divide-and-conquer behaves like merge sort.

items.prompt:
What is the running time of this code?
`for i in range(n):`
`    j = 1`
`    while j < n:`
`        j *= 2`

options.label: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)

rubric: The inner loop doubles j, so it runs about log n times, and it runs once per outer iteration: n log n.
O(n^2) treats the doubling loop as linear.

items.prompt: Using dynamic programming, what is the minimum number of coins from denominations {1, 4, 5} needed to make 8?
rubric: The DP table gives best(8)=best(4)+1=2 via 4+4.
4 is the greedy result 5+1+1+1, which is not optimal for this coin set.

items.prompt: A graph has edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, C-E, D-F, E-F, and neighbours are taken in alphabetical order. In which order does a breadth-first search from A visit the vertices?

options.label: A, C, B, E, D, F
A, B, C, E, D, F
A, B, C, D, E, F
A, B, D, F, C, E

rubric: BFS uses a FIFO queue: level 1 is B, C; level 2 is D, E; then F.
A, B, D, F, C, E is a depth-first order.

items.prompt: Which of these algorithms run in O(n log n) time in the worst case on n elements? Select all that apply.

options.label: Quicksort always choosing the first element as pivot
Insertion sort
Merge sort
Heap sort

rubric: Merge sort and heap sort guarantee O(n log n) in the worst case.
First-element quicksort and insertion sort are O(n^2) in the worst case.

items.prompt: You must check whether any two numbers in a sorted array of 1,000,000 integers sum to a target. The solution must run in linear time and use O(1) extra memory. Which approach meets both constraints?

options.label: For each element, binary search the rest of the array for target minus that element
Insert each element into a hash set and check whether its complement is already there
Nested loops over all pairs, stopping at the first match found
Two pointers from both ends, moving inward by comparing the sum

rubric: Two pointers use the sorted order to be O(n) time and O(1) space.
Binary search per element is O(n log n); the hash set uses O(n) memory.

items.prompt: A binary search uses `while lo <= hi`, `mid=(lo+hi)//2`, and on `a[mid] < t` sets `lo = mid`, otherwise `hi = mid - 1`. It sometimes never terminates. What is the cause?

options.label: `lo = mid` can leave `lo` unchanged, so the range stops shrinking
`mid` is rounded down, so the midpoint can never reach the top index
The loop uses `<=` where `<` is required, so it runs once too often
`hi = mid - 1` skips the element at index `mid`, so the range collapses

rubric: With lo=4, hi=5, mid=4 and a[4]<t, lo stays 4 forever; it must be mid+1.
The other options blame the correct parts of the loop.

items.prompt: Quicksort with the last element as pivot takes minutes on an already sorted array of 200,000 items but seconds on shuffled data. What explains this?

options.label: Sorted input triggers extra swaps inside every partition step
Each partition splits off one element, giving n levels of recursion
Sorted input forces the comparisons to run more slowly each time
The recursion revisits the same subarray several times over

rubric: The last element is the maximum, so partitions are size n-1 and 0, giving O(n^2).
Distractors confuse the cost per comparison with the depth of recursion.

items.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm returns a wrong shortest distance on a graph containing one negative-weight edge. What is the underlying reason?

options.label: A vertex is finalised before a cheaper path via the negative edge is seen
The graph is certain to contain a negative cycle in that case
Relaxation only happens once per vertex, so later edges are ignored
The priority queue cannot hold a negative key without breaking

rubric: Dijkstra assumes a finalised vertex has the minimum distance, which fails when a later path can be cheaper.
A negative edge doesn't imply a negative cycle.

items.prompt: A memoised recursive DP over a sequence runs fine for n=1,000 but crashes with a stack overflow at n=100,000. An equivalent bottom-up loop works. What explains this?

options.label: Top-down DP solves more distinct subproblems than the bottom-up loop does
The memo table holds too many entries to fit in the heap at that size
Recursion depth grows with n, exceeding the call-stack limit
Memoisation makes every call do more work than an iteration of the loop

rubric: The chain of calls n deep needs n stack frames; the loop uses none.
Both versions solve the same subproblems, so work and table size are equal.

items.prompt: A function removes duplicates from a list of 100,000 items with `seen = []` and `for x in a: if x not in seen: seen.append(x)`. It is far slower than expected. What is the main cause?

options.label: The `for` loop over `a` is O(n^2) in itself
`x not in seen` scans a list, so the whole loop is O(n^2)
`append` copies the entire list every time it is called
Comparing integers is costly when many items repeat

rubric: Membership in a list is linear, executed n times, giving O(n^2); a set makes it O(1) on average.
Append is amortised O(1), and the loop itself is linear.

items.prompt: The 0/1 knapsack DP runs in O(nW) for capacity W, yet is called pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial. Which statements explain why? Select all that apply.

options.label: Running time and table size are proportional to the numeric value of W, not to the length of its encoding
DP needs recursion, which adds an exponential overhead to the work
W takes only about log W bits to write, so O(nW) is exponential in input size
DP re-solves overlapping subproblems an exponential number of times

rubric: Cost scales with the numeric value of W, which is exponential in its bit length, for both time and memory.
DP avoids recomputation and the loop version needs no recursion.

items.prompt: A service answers 100,000 lookup queries against a sorted list of 100,000 records. For each query, it scans the list from the start until it finds a match. Profiling shows 99% of time in these scans. Which change targets the dominant cost?

options.label: Rewrite the scan loop in a faster compiled language
Sort the queries first, then keep scanning from the start
Replace each scan with a binary search, cutting a query to O(log n)
Cache the results of repeated queries and keep the linear scan

rubric: Sorted data lets binary search cut total work from O(mn) to O(m log n).
A faster language only shrinks constants and caching only helps repeated queries; sorting queries doesn't change the scan cost.

items.prompt: Quicksort uses Lomuto partitioning with the last element as pivot, and `<=` pivot goes left. On an array of 100,000 identical values it takes quadratic time. What is the cause?

options.label: Every element compares as equal to the pivot, so each partition is maximally lopsided and recursion depth reaches n
Identical values make the pivot choice random, which raises the expected number of recursive calls above n log n
Equal values force the algorithm to swap each element twice per pass, doubling the constant but keeping n log n
Equal keys trigger a stack overflow that the runtime recovers from by restarting the sort on the left half

rubric: With `<=` every element lands on one side, so partitions have sizes n-1 and 0, giving O(n^2).
Distractors confuse constant factors or randomness with the structural imbalance.

items.prompt: Dijkstra's algorithm returns a wrong distance on a graph where one edge has weight -2. Which step of the algorithm's reasoning breaks?

options.label: Each edge is relaxed only once, when its source is popped, so a negative edge reached through a later path is never relaxed again
Distances are only well defined on acyclic graphs, and a negative edge usually creates a cycle that the algorithm cannot handle
A popped minimum node is treated as final, but a later path through a negative edge can still shorten it
The priority queue orders nodes by key, and negative edge weights give some nodes a wrong priority when they are inserted

rubric: Finalising a popped node relies on all remaining paths being non-negative.
Distractors blame the data structure or cycles rather than the greedy finality assumption.

items.prompt: A binary search on the answer finds the smallest capacity `c` such that `feasible(c)` is true, and feasibility is known to be monotonic. It sometimes returns a value `c` for which `feasible(c)` is false. What is the most likely flaw?

options.label: The midpoint uses integer division, which rounds down and so can stop the search one step short of the true minimum
The loop sets `lo = mid + 1` when `feasible(mid)` is false, but when it is true sets `hi = mid - 1`, which can skip the smallest feasible value and return an infeasible one
The search range starts at 1 instead of 0, which shifts each midpoint by one and so breaks the monotonic ordering of the predicate
The loop uses `lo < hi` rather than `lo <= hi`, so a range of one candidate is left unexamined, which would only matter if the answer were not already kept in `hi`

items.prompt: A function processes a list `jobs` of n items with `while jobs: job = jobs.pop(0); handle(job)`, where `handle` is O(1) and `jobs` is an array-backed list. Profiling shows quadratic growth. Why?

options.label: Removing the first element of an array-backed list shifts all remaining elements, costing O(n) per pop
`handle` is called n times, and each call adds hidden cost proportional to the number of jobs left
Each `pop(0)` reallocates the list to a smaller buffer, which copies all elements in O(n) time
The `while jobs` check scans the entire list to see whether any element is truthy on every iteration

rubric: Front removal from an array list is O(n) because of shifting, so total is O(n^2); a deque fixes it.
Distractors invent scanning or reallocation costs that do not occur.

items.prompt: A dynamic array grows by adding a fixed 10 slots whenever it is full, instead of doubling. Appending n items one at a time is analysed. What is the total copying cost?

options.label: O(n log n), because the number of growth steps shrinks logarithmically as the array gets larger
O(n sqrt n), because the fixed increment balances copying cost against the number of resizes
O(n), because each append is O(1) amortised whenever growth happens only occasionally
O(n^2), because about n/10 resizes each copy a number of items proportional to the current size

rubric: Resizes occur n/10 times, each copying up to n items, so the sum is quadratic.
Amortised O(1) needs geometric growth, which distractors wrongly assume.

items.prompt: A 0/1 knapsack DP fills a table in O(n*W) time, where n is the item count and W is the integer capacity. Which statements correctly analyse this running time? Select all that apply.

options.label: If W is bounded by a small constant, the algorithm behaves as O(n) in practice
Because the bound is polynomial in the numeric value W, it is polynomial in the input size, since W is written in unary
The table size depends only on n, so the running time is truly polynomial
Using a 1-D rolling array lowers the time complexity from O(nW) to O(W)
It is pseudo-polynomial because W grows exponentially with the number of bits used to write it

rubric: W's value is exponential in its bit length, and with constant W the cost is linear in n.
Distractors misstate input size or confuse space savings with time.

items.prompt: A BFS over a 2000x2000 grid marks cells `visited` when they are dequeued, not when they are enqueued. It returns correct distances but uses far more memory and time than expected, and the queue grows to tens of millions of entries. What explains this?

options.label: Marking on dequeue makes BFS visit cells in depth-first order, which inflates the queue with deeper cells
Marking on dequeue turns the grid into a weighted graph, so the queue must hold extra entries for tie-breaking
Marking on dequeue forces each cell to be re-expanded by every neighbour, which makes distances wrong later
Marking on dequeue lets the same cell be enqueued by several neighbours before it is processed, creating many duplicates

rubric: Cells reachable from several frontier cells are enqueued multiple times until first dequeued; marking on enqueue prevents this.
Distractors misattribute the effect to traversal order or correctness changes.

items.prompt: You must stably sort 1,000,000 records where every record is at most 8 positions from its final place. Extra memory must be O(1). Which algorithm best meets these criteria?

options.label: Insertion sort, because it is stable, in place and runs in O(n*k) time when each item is within k places
Quicksort with a random pivot, because its expected O(n log n) time beats any quadratic-style algorithm
Heapsort, because its O(n log n) worst case and in-place operation satisfy memory limits for any input order
Merge sort, because it is stable and guarantees O(n log n), which outweighs the use of a temporary buffer

rubric: Insertion sort meets stability, O(1) space and near-linear time given displacement of at most 8.
Heapsort and quicksort are unstable; merge sort needs O(n) buffer.

items.prompt: You need shortest paths from one source in a road-network graph where every edge has the same cost of 1. Criteria: lowest asymptotic time and simplest correct implementation. Which is best?

options.label: Bellman-Ford, since it tolerates unusual weights and so remains correct if costs change later on
Breadth-first search, since uniform weights make BFS order equal distance order in O(V+E) time
Dijkstra with a binary heap, since it handles every non-negative weight and so is safest for any graph
Floyd-Warshall, since it computes all pairs and so also covers the single-source case completely

rubric: BFS is O(V+E) and correct for unit weights, and simpler than heap-based methods.
Other options are valid but slower or more complex than the criteria allow.

items.prompt: A colleague argues: "Merge sort is O(n log n) worst case and quicksort is O(n^2), so always use merge sort." Judge this for in-memory arrays of primitives with randomised pivots, where memory is tight. Which critique is best?

options.label: Sound, since a worst-case bound is the only reliable basis for choosing and constants or memory are secondary concerns
Sound, since merge sort is also in place and is faster than quicksort on every input distribution
Unsound, since randomised quicksort has expected O(n log n) and sorts in place with good cache use
Unsound, since quicksort is actually O(n log n) in the worst case once a random pivot has been chosen

rubric: Randomisation makes the quadratic case vanishingly unlikely, and in-place partitioning suits tight memory.
Distractors treat worst-case bounds as absolute or misstate the properties of merge sort.

items.prompt: From a stream of 10^9 numbers you need the 100 largest, using under 1 MB memory in a single pass. Which approach best meets the criteria?

options.label: Keep a min-heap of size 100, replacing the root when a larger number arrives, in O(n log 100) time
Keep every number in a balanced tree, then walk its 100 largest nodes once the stream has ended
Keep a max-heap of all numbers seen, then pop it 100 times once the stream has ended
Sort all numbers with an external merge sort, then take the last 100 elements from the sorted output

rubric: A size-k min-heap uses O(k) memory and one pass.
The others store or sort the whole stream, breaking memory and single-pass limits.

items.prompt: A recursion has about 10^12 possible states, but for the inputs you will see only a few thousand are reachable, and depth never exceeds 200. Criteria: least work and least code. Which DP style is best?

options.label: Bottom-up tabulation with a rolling array, since memory is the only cost that matters here
Plain recursion without caching, since few reachable states mean no subproblem repeats at all
Bottom-up tabulation, since filling every state in order is always faster than recursion
Top-down memoisation, since it computes only reachable states and stays shallow within depth 200

rubric: Memoisation visits just reachable states, and depth of 200 is safe.
Tabulating 10^12 states is infeasible; skipping caching ignores overlapping subproblems.

items.prompt: You must choose an in-memory dictionary. Which requirements favour a balanced binary search tree over a hash table? Select all that apply.

options.label: A strict worst-case bound of O(log n) per operation, with no rehashing pauses
Finding the nearest smaller key to a given key
Lowest possible average cost for exact-match lookups only
Queries for all keys within a range, returned in sorted order
Keys with a cheap, well-distributed hash function available

rubric: Trees keep order, support range and predecessor queries, and give worst-case bounds.
Exact-match speed and good hashing favour hash tables.

items.prompt: A service holds 5 million static integer keys, rebuilt nightly. It must answer exact lookups and count keys in a range [a, b], with minimal memory. Which structure best meets these criteria?

options.label: A linked list kept sorted, since insertion is cheap and range counting is a simple traversal
A hash set, since exact lookup is O(1) on average and range counts can be scanned over buckets
A sorted array, since binary search finds exact keys and both range ends in O(log n) with no pointers
A balanced BST, since it supports updates and range queries even though updates are never needed here

rubric: Static data suits a sorted array: compact, binary search for lookups and range bounds.
Hash sets lack order; trees and lists add pointer overhead or linear scans.

items.prompt: An in-place Lomuto quicksort degrades to quadratic time on arrays where 90% of the keys are equal. Constraints: O(1) extra space, expected O(n log n) on such inputs, and no copy of the data. Which change best meets them?

options.label: Choose pivots uniformly at random, because random pivots stop equal keys from clustering on one side of the split
Switch to three-way partitioning, because equal keys are grouped at the pivot and left out of both recursive calls
Copy into a merge sort buffer, because merge sort is unaffected by duplicate keys and keeps the same overall cost
Use median-of-three pivot selection, because a median pivot always splits runs of equal keys into balanced halves

rubric: Three-way partitioning removes the equal block from recursion, giving linear time when all keys are equal, and stays in place.
Random or median-of-three pivots still send equal keys to one side under Lomuto; the merge sort buffer breaks the O(1) space constraint.

items.prompt: You need single-source shortest paths with nonnegative weights on a dense graph: V = 5,000 and about V^2/2 edges. Criterion: lowest worst-case running time with simple code. Which option is best?

options.label: Bellman-Ford at O(VE), because it relaxes every edge repeatedly and so handles dense graphs more reliably
Floyd-Warshall at O(V^3), because computing all pairs once covers the single source with a simple triple loop
Binary-heap Dijkstra at O((V+E) log V), because a heap finds the minimum faster than a linear scan on any graph
Array-scan Dijkstra at O(V^2), because a heap's log V factor per edge outweighs plain scans when E is near V^2

rubric: With E near V^2, heap Dijkstra costs about V^2 log V while the array version costs V^2.
Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall are slower and solve harder problems than needed; the heap-always-wins belief ignores density.

items.prompt: A colleague claims a dynamic array that grows by a fixed 16 slots whenever it is full has amortized O(1) appends, since each resize copies only a few more elements. Which critique is correct?

options.label: The claim fails, because any resize makes every append O(n) in the worst case, so amortization cannot apply at all
The claim fails, because even geometric growth only reaches O(log n) amortized cost per append, never constant
The claim fails, because total copying is about n^2/32, so amortized cost is O(n); growth must scale with current size
The claim holds, because a resize happens only once every 16 appends, so the cost per append stays bounded by a constant

rubric: Fixed increments cause copies of size 16, 32, 48, ... summing to quadratic total work; geometric growth gives O(1) amortized.
Distractors misread resize frequency as constant cost or wrongly claim geometric growth is not constant amortized.

items.prompt: A DP has 10^9 possible states (i, j), but from the start state only about 10^5 are ever reachable, and recursion depth never exceeds 60. Criterion: least running time and memory while staying safe from stack overflow. Which implementation is best?

options.label: Plain recursion without memoization, because with depth at most 60 the repeated work stays small in practice
Bottom-up tabulation over all (i, j), because iteration avoids recursion and is always faster than memoization
Top-down recursion with a hash-map memo, because only reachable states are computed and the shallow depth is safe
Bottom-up tabulation with a rolling two-row array, because it cuts memory without caring which states are reachable

rubric: Memoized recursion touches only the 10^5 reachable states, and the depth bound removes the usual stack concern.
Full tabulation visits 10^9 states; unmemoized recursion can still be exponential despite shallow depth.

items.prompt: A public API stores user-supplied string keys in a hash table using a fixed, publicly documented hash function. Criterion: keep expected total time near-linear even against an attacker crafting inputs. Which defence is best?

options.label: Seed the hash with a secret per-process random key, because attackers cannot precompute colliding strings
Replace chaining with linked lists sorted by key, because ordered chains make each colliding lookup stop early
Resize at load factor 0.5, because short average chains keep lookups fast whatever keys are inserted
Resize the table to a prime capacity, because prime sizes spread any set of keys evenly across the buckets

rubric: A secret random seed makes collisions unpredictable, defeating hash flooding.
Prime sizes, low load factors and sorted chains do not help when an attacker picks keys that all collide under a known function.

items.prompt: You must sort a 500 GB file on a machine with 16 GB RAM and a spinning disk. Which statements correctly justify choosing external merge sort over running in-memory quicksort through virtual memory? Select all that apply.

options.label: Runs are read and written sequentially, which matches the disk's high cost for random seeks
Random access into a 500 GB array is cheap on disk, so paging makes quicksort's cost the same
Sorting memory-sized runs then k-way merging needs only a few passes over the data when k is large
Merge sort uses O(1) extra memory, which is why it fits within 16 GB of RAM
Quicksort makes asymptotically more comparisons than merge sort, so it loses on every dataset

rubric: External merge sort has sequential access and a small number of passes, minimising I/O cost.
Comparison counts are not the bottleneck, random disk access is slow, and merge sort does not use O(1) space.

items.prompt: A service receives 2 billion numeric scores as a stream, can read each only once, and has under 10 MB of memory. At the end it must report the 100 largest. A teammate lists four designs. Judged against the single-pass and memory limits, which is best?

options.label: Run quickselect over an in-memory array holding all scores, then sort the 100 largest elements it finds
Keep a min-heap of the 100 largest seen so far, replacing its root when a larger score arrives
Write all scores to disk, external merge sort them, then read back the last 100 values from the sorted file
Keep every score in a max-heap, then pop 100 times, for O(n + k log n) total time and simple code

rubric: A size-k min-heap uses O(k) memory, one pass, and O(n log k) time.
The other designs store all scores or need multiple passes, violating the memory or single-read constraints.

items.prompt: Design a structure for a data stream that supports insert in O(log n) and returns the current median in O(1). Which design meets both constraints?

options.label: Keep a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half, rebalancing sizes after each insert
Keep a sorted array, find the insert position by binary search, shift later elements, then read the middle element directly
Keep one min-heap of all values and, whenever a median query arrives, pop half of the values and push them back afterwards
Keep a hash map from value to count and scan the keys in sorted order whenever the median is requested

rubric: Two balanced heaps give O(log n) inserts and a median at the root of one or both heaps.
Sorted arrays cost O(n) per insert; the other designs make queries linear or destructive.

items.prompt: Find whether any subset of 40 positive integers sums exactly to T, where T is about 10^12. Which design is feasible within time and memory limits?

options.label: Split into two halves of 20, enumerate each half's 2^20 sums, sort one list, and match complements with two pointers
Fill a DP table indexed by every reachable sum up to T, as in the classic pseudo-polynomial subset-sum table
Memoize recursion on (index, remaining target), relying on repeated states to keep the count small
Sort descending and greedily take each number that still fits, then check whether the total equals T

rubric: Meet-in-the-middle needs about 2^20 log work and memory, feasible where 2^40 and a table to 10^12 are not.
The DP table is too large, memoized states rarely repeat with huge values, and greedy is not correct for subset sum.

items.prompt: A proposed LRU cache uses a hash map from key to node, plus a singly linked list ordered by recency. Both get and put must run in O(1). What is the design missing?

options.label: A sorted array of access timestamps, so the least recent entry is found by binary search
A min-heap keyed on last access time, so the oldest entry can be removed at the top
A counter for total accesses, so each node can be stamped when it is touched
A previous pointer in each node, so a node found by the map can be unlinked in O(1)

rubric: Moving a node to the front needs its predecessor; a doubly linked list gives O(1) unlinking.
Heaps and sorted arrays cost O(log n) or O(n) for updates; a counter alone does not reorder nodes.

items.prompt: A design finds a linked-list cycle in O(1) memory using slow and fast pointers, then claims the meeting node is the cycle's first node. It must return the true start node, still in O(1) memory. What step is missing?

options.label: After meeting, store each visited node in a hash set until a repeat appears to identify the start
After meeting, move the fast pointer three nodes per step so it overtakes the slow pointer at the start
After meeting, put one pointer at the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle start
After meeting, keep advancing only the fast pointer until it reaches null, which marks the cycle start

rubric: The distance from the head to the start equals the distance from the meeting point to the start (mod cycle length), so equal-speed walking meets there.
The other options never terminate on a cycle, use O(n) memory, or have no justification.

items.prompt: Compute the maximum of every window of size k over an array of n = 10^6 numbers, with k up to 10^5. The design must run in O(n) total time. Which meets this?

options.label: A sparse table built once over the whole array, answering each window maximum with two overlapping lookups
A max-heap with lazy deletion of expired entries, popping stale tops before reading each window maximum
Recompute each window's maximum by scanning its k elements, stopping early when a large value is found
A deque of indices with decreasing values, dropping smaller ones at the back and expired ones at the front

rubric: Each index enters and leaves the deque once, so total work is O(n) and the front is always the window maximum.
Heap and sparse table are O(n log n); rescanning is O(nk) in the worst case.

items.prompt: You are designing a divide-and-conquer inversion counter for an array of 10^6 integers that must run in O(n log n) and be correct with duplicates. Which elements must the design include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Compare every left element against every right element with nested loops at each merge
Presort the array with quicksort and compare final positions to the original positions
On ties, take the left element first, so equal values are not counted as inversions
Use a 64-bit counter, since the count can reach about n^2/2, far beyond 32-bit range
During each merge, when a right-half element goes out first, add the number of remaining left-half elements

rubric: Counting remaining left elements, a wide counter and left-first ties give a correct O(n log n) merge-based count.
Nested comparisons cost quadratic time, and position comparison after sorting does not count inversions.

items.prompt: An autocomplete service holds 10^6 static strings with fixed weights. For any typed prefix it must return the 5 highest-weight completions, with latency that does not grow with the number of matching strings. Which design satisfies this?

options.label: A hash set of all strings, scanning it on every query and keeping the five best prefix matches
A trie where a query traverses the whole subtree under the prefix, then sorts all matches by weight
A sorted array of strings, using binary search to find the prefix range, then scanning that whole range with a size-5 min-heap to keep the top weights
A trie whose nodes each store a precomputed top 5, so a query walks the prefix and reads that list

rubric: Precomputing top-5 at each node makes query time proportional to prefix length only.
The other designs do work proportional to the number of matches or to the full dataset.
